basis: Independent static reverse engineering of original bytes, including decrypted source and managed CIL. No specimen, attacker task or endpoint was executed. ML and sandbox scores were leads only.

samples.marker_line: Cleaner wrapper: local launch; no hostile action established
evidence: The final IEX reconstructs Invoke-Loader from hexadecimal character codes; it calls the loader rather than a downloaded command.

Invoke-Loader decodes the embedded key, IV and ciphertext and decrypts AES-256-CBC/PKCS7. Independent decryption yields SHA-256 9716c5e7fc2bcfdba8cb667f2e5e051e83f0826e39294f4b95165f7aae0aa0e2, matching the gate before ScriptBlock.Create/source invocation.
The entire plaintext extracts archive6.zip beside the script into LOCALAPPDATA/PowershellCleaner, sleeps five seconds and starts the extracted pythonw.exe with extracted ss.py as its argument.

The supplied script establishes no stealing, spying, destruction, backdoor or user deception beyond concealing its launch instructions. Numeric obfuscation and encrypted code are suspicious capabilities, not proof that this local launch is hostile. BENIGN is the balance-of-evidence judgement for these bytes, not a judgement about the unavailable Python program.
limits: archive6.zip, ss.py and pythonw.exe are not supplied; there is no retrieval URL, versioned PURL or hash for them. No deployment history or verified publisher is available. The missing companion is not treated as proof of maliciousness or of safety.

Automatic facts recover Base64 material and numeric strings but do not decrypt the AES stage; the plaintext was independently recovered and scanned. It has zero hostile/suspicious traits and nine notable findings, including extraction, pythonw, local application data, process creation and sleep.

samples.marker_line: NjRAT Horror: TCP tasking, keylogging and boot-sector overwrite
evidence: Managed entry MethodDef 0x7a (A.main) calls OK.ko (0x43). The latter starts the OK.RC receiver thread and kl.WRK polling recorder.
OK..cctor (0x15) sets TCP host 192.168.174.1, port 8288, Victim label, protocol splitter and explicit NjRAT 0.7d Horror Edition identity. Private addressing does not make the backdoor benign.
OK.RC (0x48) reads length-framed socket data, dispatches the completed byte array through _Lambda__1 (0x17) to OK.Ind (0x40), and reconnects on failure.

kl.WRK (0x78) loops over keys 0..255, tests GetAsyncKeyState == -32767, translates/records keystrokes with active-window context in one Logs field, periodically stores the log through OK.STV, and sleeps 1 ms. The TCP command handler can retrieve the log.

OK.Ind can write and execute received/downloaded bytes, return JPEG screenshots, modify clipboard/input/UI state, schedule recurring execution, and invoke supplied managed plugins. OK.Plugin (0x46) loads its byte-array argument with Assembly.Load, walks modules and types and constructs a matching instance. New coverage records that loading capability without inventing a bound source-to-network claim.

Boot-sector command branches call MBRSlayer.Start (0x52), which opens PhysicalDrive0 with generic-all access and passes a 512-byte boot payload to WriteFile at the initial file position. Its commands may require administrator rights; static hostile intent does not require success.

The active unprompted recorder and network command surface, including destructive tasking, outweigh a hypothetical authorized lab use. No supplied authorization or analysis-tool packaging explains it. Triage independently extracts the matching configuration and family identity.
limits: All install, anti-analysis, Defender/UAC-disable and critical-process options initialized Disabled/False must be distinguished from enabled execution. The corresponding strings/capabilities remain accurately detected; active startup evasion is not claimed.
Actual deployment, operator authorization and successful C2 communication are unavailable. The review establishes behavior and tasking capability statically; no victim damage is claimed.

samples.identification: Self-contained managed ransom locker and spyware, xoilac66-tv.online_hyber assembly
samples.marker_line: Ransom spyware: keylog POST, credential theft and recovery sabotage
evidence: Entry MethodDef 0x1a (Program.Main) creates work/log/screenshot/stolen-data directories, marks the work directory hidden/system, shows a topmost ransom form, calls BlockInput(true), and starts surveillance and installation workers.

StartKeylogger (0x25) installs WH_KEYBOARD_LL with HookCallback (0x26). The WM_KEYDOWN callback reads the virtual key and appends timestamped Keys values to the key log. ContinuousDataExfiltration.MoveNext (0xa2) reads key and clipboard log deltas and calls SendToC2.

SendToC2.MoveNext (0xa4) serializes records into a data form field and supplies FormUrlEncodedContent to HttpClient.PostAsync at the configured http://xoilac66-tv.online endpoint. No endpoint was contacted during this review.

ContinuousScreenshot (0x28) captures the primary screen and writes JPEGs. ClipboardMonitor.MoveNext (0x85) reads a clipboard handle, locks it, converts it to a string and appends a changed-value record. Its request uses CF_TEXT=1 but PtrToStringUni; successful text decoding is not assumed.

ReadBrowserData (0x35) copies Chrome Default Cookies, History and Login Data to stolen-data files. StealCookies.MoveNext (0x93) reads the Cookies file, Base64-encodes/truncates its bytes and sends a cookie record to SendToC2. This is store-byte theft, not proof of decrypted passwords.

AccessWindowsCredentialManager (0x34) constructs LocalApplicationData/Microsoft/Credentials, enumerates its files and copies them to cred_backup. It does not decrypt credential blobs. This previously lacked the matching hostile objective.

InstallPersistence (0x24), CreateStartupBat (0x3f) and MorePersistence (0x4b) install Run/RunOnce references, Startup self-launch files, an onlogon scheduled task and a daily task. PDF association hijacking and removable-drive self-copy/autorun code provide additional activation paths.

DisableSafeMode, DisableSystemRestore and DeleteShadowCopies modify recovery settings and launch VSS/WMIC deletion commands. Other methods stop/disable security services, issue Defender-disable commands, change firewall policy, append security-vendor hosts sinkholes, and attempt the fodhelper/DelegateExecute hijack.

RealEncryption.MoveNext (0x81) enumerates Desktop/TestFolder recursively, then attempts read -> EncryptAES -> suffixed WriteAllBytes -> Delete(original). EncryptAES (0x21) assigns UTF-8 HiddenTearsKey123 (17 bytes) to AES.Key and H1ddenT3ars1v!! (15 bytes) to AES.IV. The invalid key assignment throws before IV assignment, encryption, replacement or source deletion; per-file exceptions are swallowed. The ransom note falsely says AES-256 encryption succeeded. Preserve attempted encryption and extortion; do not assert broad successful file encryption.

AdditionalBlacklistedRequests (0x6f) calls GetAsync and Wait and discards responses. Launch paths elsewhere run self-copies, system commands or generated helper scripts. There is no downloaded-byte/file-to-process execution chain here; the original dropper finding was unsupported.

Method names, fabricated malware-family mutexes, genesis Bitcoin address and simulation log text are not family attribution or authorization. The recorder sends input without a consent gate, credential-store copying and host-wide security/recovery sabotage extend beyond TestFolder, and the executable falsely poses as encrypted-file recovery. These concrete operations tip the judgement to MALICIOUS even though some routines are broken or demonstrative.
limits: No runtime encryption success, remote payload execution, credential decryption, real cross-host network spreading or attribution to BlackCat/HiddenTear is claimed. NetworkSpread only targets localhost/127.0.0.1 administrative shares.

No genuine document exploit is established by appended Base64 PDF text. The PDF association command is an implemented local activation mechanism. ProcessInjection uses a trivial stub; referenced debugger APIs alone do not establish an enabled anti-debugger branch.

remaining_disagreement.classifier: PowerShell remains ML HOSTILE (0.9991268) despite zero hostile rules and no concrete hostile action in the recovered source. This is a classifier false-positive disagreement; no sample-specific exception or score-shaping duplicate was added. Both PE classifiers agree with MALICIOUS.
remaining_disagreement.material_detection_losses: None supported. The generic PowerShell concealment finding remains suspicious; the falsely linked dropper is retained as a neutral API profile; the suffix-encryption and network-tool observations preserve their predicates after relocation.
remaining_disagreement.coverage_limits: The AES plaintext is not automatically exposed as a scan child; its extraction and Python launch are found when scanned separately. Managed method-to-method value flow is not available in cleave facts (only the CLR entry import is projected), so the new CIL capabilities and collection composite explicitly limit their claims. Both malicious samples exceed the hostile coverage goal across distinct objectives; no invented family, successful encryption or remote execution claim fills an evidence gap.
